reading.title: Convenience Should Not Erase Student Privacy
reading.purpose: Weigh an argument about protecting personal privacy in an era of smart software.
paras: Modern schools and towns love tools that automate daily tasks, letting software run roll calls, bus routes, or lunch lines with little hand work. Used well, smart code saves real time. Yet ease has a steep cost when each tap feeds round-the-clock surveillance, the nonstop tracking of where people go and what they read. Guarding basic privacy—the right to keep personal space and data out of public view—should count just as much as speed.

Inside most free apps sits an algorithm, a step-by-step set of rules picking which clips, ads, or posts show up next. Since these tools prize clicks, flashy misinformation—false or skewed claims shared online—can proliferate fast, spreading across feeds before people check the facts. Even artificial faces and voices built by code now blur the line between real news and slick fakes in virtual rooms.

Fans of tracking say data makes apps smooth and claim users agree by clicking "Accept." That view misses what true consent needs: free permission from someone who grasps the terms. A teen facing a forty-page legal wall cannot give real permission in three seconds. People also need space to ask hard questions or browse books in an anonymous way, without every search tied for life to their real name.
We do not have to ban tech to set fair rules. Schools and towns should demand plain choices and firm caps on saved student data. Smart tools should serve people—not watch them in the dark.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "proliferate" most nearly means
choices: to disappear quietly after a single fact-check
to multiply quickly and spread widely across feeds
to follow step-by-step rules inside a lunch line
to ask for clear permission before saving user data
qs.why: Paragraph 2 restates proliferate directly as "multiplying across feeds before anyone checks the facts."

qs.q: Which sentence explains why clicking "Accept" on a long legal page is not real consent?
choices: Fans of tracking say data makes apps smooth and claim users agree by clicking "Accept."
That view misses what true consent needs: free permission from someone who grasps the terms.
A teen facing a forty-page legal wall cannot give real permission in three seconds.
We do not have to ban tech to set fair rules.
qs.why: This sentence gives the concrete reason: a teen cannot meaningfully understand forty pages of legal text in three seconds.

ev.text: A teen facing a forty-page legal wall cannot give real permission in three seconds.

qs.q: What is the author's overall attitude toward modern technology?
choices: Technology is useful when paired with clear privacy rules and honest user choices.
Schools should ban all computers, bus software, and online libraries immediately.
Algorithms are completely harmless as long as students read forty-page agreements.
Constant digital tracking is necessary so attendance and lunch lines move faster.
qs.why: Paragraph 1 praises smart uses of automation and paragraph 4 says "We do not have to reject technology to set fair boundaries."

qs.q: What is the author's main claim in this argument?
choices: Free apps should stop showing videos because virtual spaces are too confusing.
Speed and convenience from digital tools should not come at the cost of privacy and real consent.
Lawmakers should forbid students from browsing library topics without using their real names.
Artificial voices are the only serious threat facing middle school students online.
qs.why: The essay argues that automation and helpful software must be balanced with strong privacy limits, plain-language consent, and room for anonymity.

clues.text: the nonstop tracking of where people go and what they read
false or skewed claims shared online
free permission from someone who grasps the terms
